title: Session Spline — UX sprint notes and rough PRD
content:
One-liner:
Session Spline = a lightweight, adaptive session summarization and slice system that creates compact, editable context artifacts ("splines") to reduce token cost while preserving enough semantics for high-quality responses across long conversations.

Problem space / motivating signals:
- We've seen rising per-session token spikes for power users and long-running workflows (multi-turn design reviews, coding sessions, tutoring). Costs and tail latency spike when clients send entire transcripts back and forth.
- Current approaches (full transcript, naive summarization) either keep too much verbatim context or produce brittle global summaries that drift.
- Product teams want a knob between "full fidelity" and "cheap but lossy" that is transparent to end users and reversible (users can expand compressed context).

Hypothesis / value prop:
If we surface a session-level, structured compression artifact that is incremental and editable, apps can:
  - Reduce average tokens per request by 30–60% for long sessions,
  - Retain deterministic recall for important facts (entities, instructions, state), and
  - Give users control to expand or pin parts of the transcript to full fidelity when needed.

Primary personas:
- Product engineers integrating Redwood API into chat/assistant flows (care about latency/cost).
- Power end-users (customer support reps, dev pairs, tutors) who maintain long-running sessions with repeated references.
- Platform/ops engineers who want predictable token volume for billing/SLA forecasting.

User scenarios (concrete):
1) Long design critique: designer and PM run a 90-minute thread referencing earlier sketches; the assistant should answer targeted questions while avoiding re-sending whole transcript every call.
2) Pair-programming session: code snippets, line references, and running context need to be preserved; developer sometimes wants to expand prior snippet to resolve ambiguity.
3) Customer support multi-touch: tickets include facts (account id, steps tried) that must be retained but verbose logs can be compressed.

Goals / success metrics (MVP):
- Reduce tokens-per-session (average payload tokens) by >=40% on internal benchmark for sessions >2k tokens.
- No more than 5% regression in task-level quality (measured by automated evals + human spot-check) vs full-transcript baseline.
- UX: users can expand any spline section within 2 clicks; pinning a section prevents compression.

Non-goals (initial):
- Not building a full semantic search index across splines (out of scope for MVP).
- No enterprise encryption/HSM-specific UX changes (defer to private-deployments track).

MVP feature set (rough):
- Local client SDK: create/update/expand spline APIs (REST + SDK helpers).
- Server-side compressor: incremental summarization model that emits "spline blocks" with metadata (timestamp, tokens saved, importance score, anchors).
- Expand/pin endpoints: returning original excerpt(s) when requested.
- Simple UI affordances (client-side): show compressed chips in conversation, click-to-expand, pin toggle.

Data model sketch (textual):
- spline_id: opaque id
- blocks: list of {anchor_span, compressed_text, importance_tags, source_message_ids, version}
- user_pins: list of message ids that are excluded from compression
- footprint: tokens_before, tokens_after, savings_pct
(Implementation note: keep model simple — store source message ids to allow deterministic expansion; avoid heavy embedding indexes for MVP)

User stories (prioritized):
- As a product engineer, I want an SDK call that returns a session payload with spline metadata so I can decide what to send to the model. (Acceptance: SDK returns content + blocks + savings estimate)
- As an end-user, I want to click compressed chips to see the original text so I can verify context. (Acceptance: expansion returns original 3–5 messages inline)
- As an admin, I want to see token savings per session in console so we can measure impact. (Acceptance: console shows per-session tokens_before/after)

Quality guardrails / safety considerations:
- Avoid hallucinated "summaries" that invent facts. Compression should prefer extraction + conservative abstraction.
- Keep trace to source content so we can surface provenance during human review.
- Respect redaction rules (if a message is redacted, do not include it in compressed output).

Experiments & evaluation plan:
- Offline eval: run compressor on 1,000 sampled long sessions (varied domains). Measure ROUGE/precision for fact retention vs human-annotated key facts. Compute token savings and automated answer equivalence on a downstream QA probe.
- Online A/B: 5% traffic for power-user cohort with savings threshold (>=35% token reduction). Monitor latency, user expand rate, and complaint signal.

Open questions / design tradeoffs (brain dump):
- Compression strategy: extraction-first (safer) vs abstractive (denser). MVP leans extraction-then-abstraction with a short rewrite step.
- Where to run: client-side micro-compressor (fast) or server-side (more consistent)? Maybe hybrid: local prefilter + server consolidate.
- How to surface 'importance score' meaningfully in the UI without confusing users?
- Rollout: per-user default off, power-users opt-in; consider opt-out toggles for enterprise.

Implementation sketch & timeline (6-week sprint cadence):
- Week 0–2: proto compressor + data model, SDK hooks, local UX mockups (internal).
- Week 3–4: integrate expand/pin endpoints, console metrics, offline eval.
- Week 5: small closed beta with internal teams + one customer.
- Week 6: iterate on faults, prepare A/B for limited public traffic.

Next steps / TODOs (immediate):
- Align with SRE on storage costs for storing source spans (Devon).
- Build minimal SDK surface for JS + Python (Hanae).
- Draft evaluation rubric and gather 500 candidate sessions from support and design teams (Rowan).
- Create Confluence page with evaluation templates and privacy checklist (link: CONF-2319).

Notes to self / loose ideas:
- Could combine with prefix caching: treat pinned regions as cache keys.
- Consider a compact binary representation for splines for on-device storage (later).
- Keep UX reversible — users hate irreversible lossy compression.

Quick risk log:
- Risk: users expand too often => no savings. Mitigation: show savings estimate and make expansion transient (doesn't auto-expand for subsequent calls).
- Risk: hallucination introduced by abstractive summarize. Mitigation: provenance + conservative rewrite.

End of notes — this doc is a living work-in-progress. Will convert into a short PRD and attached proto types once we get alignment on evaluation targets.
